summary: Gives best practices for writing specifications that use HTTP as a base for new application protocols. It is mainly meant to guide IETF efforts for protocols deployed on the Internet, though it may suit other situations. It is a Best Current Practice and obsoletes RFC 3205.

plainLanguage.summary: Many non-browser applications send their data over HTTP, because it is well understood and everything already supports it. This document gives advice to the people writing the specification of such an application, so that clients and servers built by different teams still work together.

subtitle: Best practices for specifying new application protocols that run on top of HTTP.

tldr.problem: Applications that run on HTTP are often written for one deployment and a few clients, and fall apart when several teams build separate implementations that must still work together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC is a set of best practices: express application meaning in resources, media types and header fields, use the registered methods and status codes, discover URLs through links and well-known URIs, and set caching and security behaviour deliberately.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 3205, written to guide IETF efforts to define application protocols deployed on the Internet. It registers nothing and defines no protocol of its own.

today: RFC 9205 is a Best Current Practice published in June 2022. It obsoleted RFC 3205 and has not been obsoleted since. The advice reflects HTTP as it stood in 2022; the document notes that the changes from RFC 3205 were too numerous to list individually.

sections.title: Why Protocols Are Built on HTTP
sections.content:
Applications other than web browsing often use HTTP as a substrate, a practice sometimes called creating 'HTTP-based APIs', 'REST APIs', or just 'HTTP APIs'. The reasons are practical: implementers, specifiers, administrators, developers and users are familiar with it; client, server and proxy implementations exist; it is easy to use; web browsers exist; mechanisms such as authentication and encryption can be reused; HTTP servers and clients are already present in target deployments; and it can traverse firewalls.

Such protocols are often ad hoc, intended for deployment by one or a few servers and consumption by a limited set of clients, and a body of practices and tools has grown up around those conditions. The mismatch appears when an application has multiple separate implementations, is deployed on multiple uncoordinated servers and is consumed by diverse clients, as is often the case for HTTP APIs defined by standards efforts. Clients and servers then implement and evolve at different paces, so deployments with different features and versions have to coexist.

The document answers the design questions an application protocol built on HTTP faces: whether to define a new URI scheme or new ports, whether to use the standard HTTP methods and status codes or define new ones, how to get the most out of HTTP, how to coexist with other uses of HTTP such as web browsing, and how to avoid interoperability problems and protocol dead ends. It is written primarily to guide IETF efforts to define application protocols using HTTP for deployment on the Internet, and its requirements do not necessarily apply to the development of generic HTTP extensions. It obsoletes RFC 3205 to reflect what has changed since then.
sections.plainLanguage: Many non-browser applications send their data over HTTP, because it is well understood and everything already supports it. This document gives advice to the people writing the specification of such an application, so that clients and servers built by different teams still work together.

sections.title: When the Recommendations Apply
sections.content:
The recommendations apply when a specification defines an application that uses the transport port 80 or 443, or uses the URI scheme 'http' or 'https', or uses an ALPN protocol ID that generically identifies HTTP, such as 'http/1.1', 'h2' or 'h3', or makes registrations in or overall modifications to the IANA registries defined for HTTP. When a specification is using HTTP, all of the requirements of the HTTP protocol suite are in force. The document is aimed at applications rather than at generic extensions to HTTP, and other standards organisations are encouraged to follow it.

An application can rely on HTTP without meeting those criteria. It might want to avoid re-specifying parts of the message format while changing other aspects of the protocol's operation, or it might want to use application-specific methods. Doing so permits more freedom to modify protocol operations, but at least part of the benefit is lost, because most HTTP implementations will not adapt easily to such changes, and the benefit of mindshare is lost as well.

Such specifications MUST NOT use HTTP's URI schemes, transport ports, ALPN protocol IDs or IANA registries; rather, they are encouraged to establish their own.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice applies when your application uses the usual HTTP ports, the http or https schemes, or the HTTP ALPN identifiers, or when it changes the HTTP registries. If you only borrow parts of HTTP, you are on your own and should define your own scheme, port and registry entries.

sections.title: What Is Important About HTTP
sections.content:
Much of the value of HTTP lies in its generic semantics: the protocol elements it defines are potentially applicable to every resource and are not specific to one context. Application-specific semantics are best expressed in message content and header fields, not in status codes or methods. That split lets an HTTP message be handled by common software such as servers, intermediaries, client implementations and caches without those implementations understanding the application, and it lets people reuse their knowledge of HTTP. Applications that use HTTP MUST NOT redefine, refine or overlay the semantics of generic protocol elements such as methods, status codes or existing header fields; they should focus on their own resources.

Specifications also often say exactly how HTTP is to be implemented and used, which easily creates an unintended profile of behaviour. A rule such as 'a POST request MUST result in a 201 (Created) response' forms an expectation in the client that the response will always be 201, when in reality a proxy might require authentication, a server-side error might occur, or a redirection might happen. A client that does not anticipate that has a brittle deployment.

The second property is links. Assuming that a server's URL space belongs exclusively to one application overlays special semantics on that space and stops other applications from using it. As BCP 190 explains, such squatting on part of the URL space usurps the server's authority over its own resources, causes deployment issues and is bad practice in standards. Instead of statically defining URI components such as paths, applications using HTTP are RECOMMENDED to define and use links. Links let a request be routed to a different server without the overhead of a redirection, let different applications be mixed on the same server, offer a natural mechanism for extensibility, versioning and capability management because the document containing the links can describe their targets, and provide a form of cache invalidation: when a resource's state changes, the application changes the affected links so a fresh copy is fetched.

The third property is rich functionality: message framing, multiplexing in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, integration with TLS, support for intermediaries such as proxies, gateways and content delivery networks, client authentication, content negotiation for format and language, caching for scalability and for reduced latency and bandwidth, granularity of access control through a rich space of URLs, partial content, and the ability to interact with the application easily using a web browser. The document requires no specific feature, since the right trade-offs depend on the situation, but it encourages applications to use them.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP's value is that its parts mean the same thing everywhere, so ordinary servers, caches and proxies can handle any application built on it. The document says to add meaning in your own resources and header fields, not by changing what methods or status codes mean, and to point at resources with links rather than fixing paths.

sections.title: Specifying Server Behaviour, Client Behaviour and URLs
sections.content:
Server-side behaviour is most effectively specified by defining media types, HTTP header fields, and the behaviour of resources identified by link relations. Composing those elements defines a set of resources that implement specified behaviour: retrieval of resource state using GET in one or more formats identified by media type; resource creation or update using POST or PUT with an identified request content format; data processing using POST with identified request and response content formats; and resource deletion using DELETE. The RFC's example says that resources linked to with the 'example-widget' link relation type are Widgets, that a Widget's state can be fetched in the 'application/example-widget+json' format and updated by PUT to the same link, that Widget resources can be deleted, and that the 'Example-Count' response header field says how many Widgets the sender holds. Applications can also specify the use of URI Templates so that clients can generate URLs from runtime data.

Client expectations ought to be aligned with those of web browsers, and the RFC suggests defining them in terms of Fetch, the abstraction browsers use for HTTP. Some client behaviours, such as automatic redirect handling, and extensions such as cookies are not required by HTTP but have become common, so applications should say explicitly what they expect: how redirects are handled, an explicit reference to the Cookie specification if cookies are required, and that TLS certificates are checked according to the HTTP specification when HTTPS is used. Applications should not require that clients statically support features that are usually negotiated, such as a particular content coding, because otherwise conformant clients cannot interoperate.

For URLs, parts of the URL space are meant to be under the control of the server owner, so a specification will usually not contain fixed application URLs or paths. Although it is common for a single-deployment API to fix a path prefix such as '/app/v1', doing that in an IETF specification is inappropriate. A client generally starts by requesting an initial document that describes that deployment and may contain links to other resources, which keeps the deployment flexible and lets the server tailor the document to the client. The initial URL can be configured in full, or derived from the server's hostname and the application's identity. For the latter case the RFC lists two strategies: register a well-known URI as an entry point, which gives a fixed path on every potential server that will not collide with other applications, or let the server authority convey a URI Template or similar mechanism for generating the entry point URL.

For the URI scheme, applications will typically use 'http' and/or 'https', and 'https' is RECOMMENDED to provide authentication, integrity and confidentiality and to mitigate pervasive monitoring attacks. Application-specific schemes are possible but carry caveats: unmodified browsers will not support them, existing clients, intermediaries and caches will not recognise them, automatically generated URLs can leak the old scheme, the resources remain reachable over 'http' and 'https' anyway, and features that rely on the URL's origin, such as the same-origin policy, are affected by a change of scheme. For transport ports, an application can use the default ports, 80 for HTTP and 443 for HTTPS, or be deployed on other ports, a decision made at deployment time or encouraged by registering a port. A non-default port has to appear in the authority of all the URLs for that resource, and it has privacy implications, because the protocol can then be distinguished from other traffic, as well as operability concerns, because some networks may block it.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol built on HTTP is defined by its resources, its media types and its header fields, not by new methods. Clients find the starting URL from a well-known path or from the server itself, and the document explains why a new scheme or a new port costs more than it seems to.

sections.title: Methods, Status Codes and Redirects
sections.content:
Applications that use HTTP MUST confine themselves to registered methods such as GET, POST, PUT, DELETE and PATCH. New methods are rare, must be registered in the HTTP Method Registry with IETF Review, and must be generic, meaning potentially applicable to all resources. While some applications historically defined application-specific methods, HTTP now forbids this, and a proposal for a new method should be raised as a separate HTTP extension rather than inside an application's specification.

GET is the most common and useful method: its retrieval semantics allow caching and side-effect free linking and underlie many of the benefits of HTTP. Queries can be performed with GET, often using the query component of the URL, and the results can be cached, which improves an often expensive process. GET can be unwieldy for large queries, because binary data has to be encoded to fit the URI syntax and some implementations limit the size of URLs they support, although modern HTTP software typically supports considerably more than 8000 octets. An application might then use POST to express queries in the request content, avoiding encoding overhead and URL length limits, but the benefits of GET such as caching and linking to query results are lost, so such applications ought to allow both methods. Processing of GET requests should not change the application's state or have other significant side effects, because implementations can and do retry failed GET requests, and some GET requests protected by TLS early data might be vulnerable to replay attacks.

OPTIONS was defined for metadata retrieval and is used by WebDAV and CORS, so it is often considered for HTTP APIs, but it has significant limitations: it cannot be linked to with a simple URL because OPTIONS is not the default method; OPTIONS responses are not cacheable because caches operate on GET and HEAD representations; it is 'chatty', increasing the number of requests needed; and implementation support is not universal, so some servers cannot answer OPTIONS without significant effort. The RFC suggests alternatives: a well-known URI for server-wide metadata, or a separate resource linked to with a Link response header field or serialised into the content for metadata about a specific resource.

Status codes convey semantics for caches, intermediaries and clients as well as for applications, and applications run into pitfalls with them. Status codes are often generated by components other than the application: network errors, a captive portal, a proxy, a content delivery network, an overloaded server, or generic client software. Mapping application errors one-to-one onto status codes exhausts the finite space of applicable codes and leads to bad practices, such as minting new application-specific codes. Instead, applications should use the most applicable status code and make generous use of the general ones, 200, 400 and 500, when in doubt, without specifying a one-to-one relationship, and should convey finer-grained error information in the message content and header fields. Clients ought to be able to handle all applicable status codes gracefully, falling back to the generic semantics of a class, such as handling 499 as 400. Applications MUST NOT re-specify the semantics of status codes, even by copying their definition, and it is NOT RECOMMENDED to require specific reason phrases, because the reason phrase has no function in HTTP, is not guaranteed to be preserved by implementations, and is not carried at all in the HTTP/2 message format.

The 3xx status codes direct the user agent to another resource, and the common ones, 301, 302, 307 and 308, all use the Location response header field. They differ in two ways: whether they are permanent or temporary, which determines whether a client may update stored links, and whether they allow the redirected request to change the method from POST to GET. Browsers generally do change POST to GET for 301 and 302, so 308 and 307 were created to allow redirection without changing the method. A user agent may automatically follow a 3xx redirect that has a Location header field even without understanding the status code, but is not required to, so an application that wants redirects followed has to specify the circumstances. Redirects can be cached when the right cache directives are present, but they are not 'sticky': redirecting one URI does not mean similar URIs will also be redirected. Applications are encouraged to specify that 301 and 302 change a subsequent POST, but no other method, to GET, to stay compatible with browsers.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the methods HTTP already has, and treat status codes as a general-purpose set rather than one code per error. The document explains the four redirect codes, and why a request that changes the server's state should not be a GET.

sections.title: Caching, State and Ordering
sections.content:
HTTP caching is one of the primary benefits of using HTTP: it provides scalability, reduces latency and improves reliability, and caches are readily available in browsers, in networks as forward and reverse proxies, in content delivery networks and in server software. Even an application not designed to use caching has to consider how caches will handle its responses, so that behaviour stays correct when a cache is interposed.

Assigning even a short freshness lifetime, such as 5 seconds, lets a response be reused to satisfy several clients or one client repeating the same request. The most common way to state freshness is the max-age response directive; the Expires header field can also be used but is unnecessary, since all modern cache implementations support Cache-Control, and stating freshness as a delta is usually more convenient and less error-prone. The public directive is only needed when it is desirable to store an authenticated response, or when the status code is not understood by the cache and there is no explicit freshness information. Without explicit freshness directives a cache may store a response and serve it with a heuristic lifetime that the application does not control, so it is generally preferable to set an explicit lifetime or to make the response explicitly uncacheable. When caching is not wanted, the right directive is no-store; the no-cache directive allows a response to be stored but not reused without validation.

Stale responses can be reused by caches when disconnected from the origin server, which is useful for handling network trouble, and when that is not suitable the origin should send the must-revalidate directive. Stale responses can be refreshed by assigning a validator, which saves bandwidth and latency for large responses. If an application has a lifetime of its own, separate from the freshness lifetime, it should be conveyed separately and the relationship with caching considered carefully, because the response will be used as long as it is considered fresh; one way to handle this is to specify that responses need to be fresh upon use. If a request header field changes the response, the resource should either make its responses uncacheable or send the Vary response header field on all responses from that resource, including the default response.

Applications can use stateful cookies to identify a client or store client-specific data that contextualises requests. When they do, the scoping and use of cookies must be specified carefully, because if the application exposes sensitive data or capabilities, for example by acting as an ambient authority, exploits are possible; a mitigation is a request-specific token that ensures the intent of the client.

Clients often need several requests for one task. In HTTP/1, parallel requests are most often supported by opening multiple connections, and too many simultaneous connections hurt performance because their congestion control is not coordinated. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 offer multiplexing instead, but performance still depends on how the server prioritises responses, so either the server determines the priority or the client hints its priorities. In all versions of HTTP, requests are made independently, and the relative order of two requests cannot be relied on to guarantee the order of their processing, because they might be sent over a multiplexed protocol by an intermediary or to different origin servers, or processed in a different order. If two requests need strict ordering, the only reliable way to ensure the outcome is to issue the second request when the final response to the first has begun. Applications MUST NOT make assumptions about the relationship between separate requests on a single transport connection, because doing so breaks many of the assumptions of HTTP as a stateless protocol and causes problems with interoperability, security, operability and evolution.
sections.plainLanguage: Caching is one of the main reasons to build on HTTP, and the document says how to tell caches when a response may be reused and when it may not. It also warns that HTTP gives no ordering guarantee between two requests, so an application that needs them in sequence must wait for the first answer to start arriving.

sections.title: Browsers, Application Boundaries, Server Push and Versioning
sections.content:
Even when an application is not meant to be used with a web browser, its resources remain available to browsers and other HTTP clients, so it has to consider how browsers will interact with them, particularly regarding security. If an application's state can be changed with a POST request, a web browser can easily be coaxed into cross-site request forgery from arbitrary web sites. If an attacker gains control of content returned by the application's resources, for example because part of the request is reflected in the response, they can inject code into the browser and access data and capabilities as if they were the origin, which is a cross-site scripting attack.

The document's advice is to consider the application as a web application and follow best practices for secure development. Some of the measures it names are: using an application-specific media type in the Content-Type header field and requiring clients to fail if it is not used; using X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff so that content under attacker control cannot be coaxed into being treated as active content; using Content-Security-Policy to constrain the capabilities of active content; using Referrer-Policy to prevent sensitive data in URLs from being leaked in the Referer request header field; using the 'HttpOnly' flag on cookies so that they are not exposed to browser scripting languages; and avoiding compression on sensitive information such as authentication tokens and passwords, because the scripting environment offered by web browsers allows an attacker to repeatedly probe the compression space and, with access to the network path, to recover that information.

Many HTTP capabilities are scoped to the origin, so applications also have to consider how they interact with other applications on the same origin server. If cookies carry application state they are sent with all requests to the origin by default, unless scoped by path, and an application might receive cookies belonging to other applications, which can cause security issues as well as collisions in cookie names. One solution is a dedicated hostname for the application, but it is often desirable to allow several applications on one hostname because that gives the most deployment flexibility. Applications should therefore not mandate the use of a particular cookie name, HTTP authentication realm or other origin-wide mechanism, but let deployments configure them, and should consider scoping them to part of the origin. Applications that wish to expose cross-origin data to browsers need to implement the CORS protocol.

HTTP/2 added server push, which seems to fit many application semantics, but the RFC lists the caveats: it is hop by hop and so is not forwarded automatically by intermediaries such as proxies, reverse proxies and content delivery networks; it can have a negative performance impact when it contends with resources the client actually requested; clients implement it differently, especially regarding caching; there is no current browser API for it; it is not supported in HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/1.0; and it does not form part of the core semantics of HTTP, so a future version might not support it. Applications that can do work before the full response is available may benefit from the 103 (Early Hints) status code instead, and applications using server push directly need to enforce the authority requirements to avoid cross-origin push attacks.

Finally, new features and changes are introduced by using a distinct link relation type to identify a URL for a resource that implements the new functionality, a distinct media type to identify formats that enable it, or a distinct HTTP header field to implement it outside the message content.
sections.plainLanguage: Browsers will reach an application's resources whether it wants them to or not, so the document lists the ways that goes wrong and the headers that help. It also covers sharing a server with other applications, the limits of server push, and how to add new features later without breaking old clients.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Applications using HTTP are subject to the security considerations of HTTP itself and of any extensions used; the HTTP semantics, HTTP caching and Web linking specifications are often relevant. The recommendation to support 'https' URLs is there to provide authentication, integrity and confidentiality and to mitigate pervasive monitoring attacks. Many applications perform authentication and authorisation with bearer tokens, for example in session cookies, and if the transport is unencrypted an attacker who can eavesdrop on or modify the traffic can often escalate their privileges to act on resources. The document also points at the potential mismatch between HTTP caching and application-specific storage of responses, the effect of using stateful mechanisms in the protocol as ambient authority, the implications of web browsers' capabilities, the issues that arise when an application is deployed on the same origin as websites and other applications, and the risks of using HTTP/2 server push in a manner other than that specified.

An application that needs modifications to HTTP implementations, for example requiring support for a new URI scheme or a non-standard method, risks those implementations forking from their parent HTTP implementations, with the possible result that they do not benefit from patches and other security improvements incorporated upstream.

On privacy, HTTP clients expose a variety of information to servers. Besides information sent explicitly as part of the application's operation and what travels on the wire, other information can be gathered through less obvious means, often by connecting a user's activities over time. That includes session information, such as the client's IP address, TLS session tickets, cookies and ETags stored in the client's cache, and other stateful mechanisms; applications are advised to avoid session mechanisms unless they are unavoidable or necessary for operation, in which case the risks need to be documented, and implementations should be encouraged to allow clearing such state. Fingerprinting uses unique aspects of a client's messages and behaviour to connect disparate requests, for example the User-Agent request header field and the Accept-Language request header field, so applications are advised to specify that clients should only emit the information they need to function. Finally, an application that exposes the ability to execute code has to be careful, because observing the environment can be used to fingerprint the client and to obtain and manipulate private data, including session information; access to high-resolution timers can even profile the underlying hardware and create a unique identifier for the system.
sections.plainLanguage: The document collects the security and privacy points that follow from running an application over HTTP: use https, watch what state you keep on clients, send only the headers you need, and treat any feature that executes code on the client with care.

viz.caption: Why the RFC steers applications away from OPTIONS

items.title: Not linkable
items.text: It cannot be linked to with a simple URL because OPTIONS is not the default method.

items.title: Not cacheable
items.text: Caches work on GET and HEAD representations, so OPTIONS responses are not cached.

items.title: Chatty
items.text: Requesting metadata separately increases the number of requests needed.

items.title: Not universally supported
items.text: Some servers cannot answer OPTIONS without significant effort.

viz.caption: The cache directives the RFC explains

items.title: max-age
items.text: States how long a response stays fresh. The most common way to give a response a freshness lifetime.

items.title: no-store
items.text: The response cannot be stored or reused by a cache.

items.title: no-cache
items.text: The response may be stored, but not reused without validation.

items.title: must-revalidate
items.text: Stale responses must not be reused when the origin cannot be reached.

items.title: public
items.text: Needed to store an authenticated response, or when the cache does not understand the status code.

items.title: Vary
items.text: Sent on every response from a resource whose content depends on a request header field.
